2.text: these youngsters become warriors? Shall I come next year?” — “All right,

3.text: come next year. Meanwhile they will grow and become stronger, some at

4.text: least.” The episode is repeated in other tales. I must mention also that the

5.text: Chukchee are described as less perfidious, and as dealing more frankly with

6.text: their enemies, than the other tribes; so that it would seem that treachery at

7.text: least is not considered as one of the virtues of war.

8.text: I was told that all kinds of incantations were used in war, but none have

9.text: been preserved in the memory of the people. A tern (Tringa Temmincki)

10.text: was considered to be a sentinel of the Chukchee tribe (čiˊčin, “looking one”),
10.resolved: čiˊčin = c+U+030C, i, U+02CA, c+U+030C, i, n
10.note: Tier-1 gloss form; lexicon lookup for ci'cin/či'čin returned no key (below the two-page floor or unattested elsewhere), keyed by hand from the raster.

11.text: because, on the approach of the enemy, it would fly up with a warning cry.

12.text: Therefore a party of warriors, when stopping for a night on the open tundra,

13.text: would apply to that bird, and ask it to guard them against a sudden attack.

14.text: A battle is a series of single fights. To be fit for fighting, every warrior

15.text: undergoes hard training, and spends all his leisure in various exercises. The

16.text: tales abound in descriptions of such exercises. The hero must run for long

17.text: distances, drawing heavily-loaded sledges. He carries stones and timber, jumps

18.text: up in the air, but, above all, he fences with his long spear. He performs

19.text: this exercise quite alone; and the chief feature of it is the brandishing of the
19.note: Draft carried a trailing comma after 'the' not present in print; checked at 2x, line ends bare before wrapping to 'spear'.

20.text: spear with the utmost force, so that it bends like a piece of raw reindeer

21.text: leg-skin. He also practises shooting with the bow, and uses for this purpose

22.text: various arrows, sharp and blunt. From all these exercises he acquires great

23.text: skill and agility. He can kill twenty men, darting from one to the other with

24.text: the swiftness of an ermine. When he is shot at, he avoids the arrows by

25.text: springing to one side, or parries them all with the butt-end of his spear, or

26.text: simply catches them between the fingers and throws them back. Only when

27.text: quite exhausted from the fatigue of fighting, can he be wounded and vanquished.

28.text: The best warriors of other tribes — for instance, of the Yukaghir — are

29.text: described in corresponding tales as catching arrows between the fingers, and

30.text: as avoiding the blows of the spear by the quickness of their motions. The

31.text: Chukchee ideal warrior is so skilled in jumping that he is almost able to fly

32.text: in the air with the birds. When paddling in a kayak, he keeps pace with a

33.text: flying gull. His build is athletic. When lying on his back, he touches the

34.text: ground only with his neck, buttocks, and heels, so thick and heavy are his

35.text: muscles. A number of Chukchee warriors are described individually. The

36.text: details of these descriptions will be given later on.

37.text: Taˊn˙ñɪm Wars. — Tales of wars may be divided into two unequal groups.

39.text: These wars took place in the interior of the territory, and the Maritime people

40.text: took little part in them. The smaller group refers to wars on the sea-coast

41.text: between the Chukchee and the Eskimo. Several interesting stories belong to

42.text: the first group, and some are even epic in character. The whole may per-

43.text: haps be considered as an embryo of a Reindeer Chukchee epos.
